title: Guillain‐Barre syndrome secondary to COVID‐19 infection: A case report
case_prompt:
A 60-year-old man with a history of pectus excavatum and no other comorbidities was brought by ambulance for a 2-day history of rapidly progressive bilateral ascending weakness, bilateral paresthesia of the hands and feet, difficulty standing, and low back pain. Three days before presentation, he had tested positive for COVID-19 and reported myalgias, fever, and nausea; he was unvaccinated. 

On neurologic examination, there was weakness of neck extension, neck flexion, and leg extension; areflexia and flaccid paralysis were noted in all four extremities. There were no bulbar or respiratory symptoms. The patient denied sensation below the level of the neck. 

The following day, muscle strength was 2/5 in both upper extremities and 2/5 in both lower extremities, with mute bilateral plantar responses. He had length-dependent loss of temperature and pain sensation in the lower extremities and hands, and absent proprioception at the toes, ankles, and knees with sparing of the proximal interphalangeal joints. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine with contrast showed diffuse enhancement and thickening of the cauda equina nerve roots, with mild enhancement of the lower thoracic and a few cervical nerve roots. 

Lumbar puncture revealed a cerebrospinal fluid protein concentration of 295 mg/dL (reference 12–60 mg/dL), a white blood cell count of 27 cells/μL (0–5 cells/μL), a red blood cell count of 1 cell/μL (0–0 cells/μL), and a glucose level of 54 mg/dL (40–70 mg/dL).
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Guillain–Barré syndrome — “Given the rapidly progressive bilateral ascending weakness; sensory loss greater in the lower extremities compared to upper extremities; severe low back pain; and EMG, LP, and MRI findings, a presumptive diagnosis of GBS was made.”  
2. Myelitis — “ruled out based on the lack of motor and sensory symptoms localized to one or more contiguous spinal cord segments, as well as lack of MRI findings consistent with the diagnosis.”  
3. Lyme disease — “ruled out with negative Lyme serology and lack of recent travel to a tick infested territory or lack of rash or lesion.”  
4. Toxin associated exposure — “ruled out given no history of reported toxin exposure.”  
5. Arbovirus infection — “ruled out on the basis of this case occurring in the winter season.”
